facts.text: At about the beginning of the Eocene the amount of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere more or less doubled.

title: Modern mammal orders appear at the Eocene's start

facts.text: The PETM warming brought more modern mammal groups into North America while many Paleocene forms declined.
The oldest fossils of most modern mammal orders appear within a brief early Eocene window, among them artiodactyls, perissodactyls and hyaenodontids.
Odd-toed ungulates seem to have arisen in Asia: Cambaytherium from western India dates to roughly 54.5 million years ago.
The new mammals had long thin legs, grasping hands and feet, and teeth differentiated for chewing.
All were small, under 10 kg; Eocene mammals were only about 60% the size of the Paleocene mammals before them.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: first rodents, lagomorphs, armadillos, sirenians, proboscideans, perissodactyls and artiodactyls c. 55 Ma

facts.text: In northern Denmark, about 60 m of diatom-rich clay with up to 180 volcanic ash layers settled on the earliest Eocene seafloor.
Deposited just after the PETM, its tropical to subtropical flora points to a climate about 4–8 °C warmer than today.
It preserves abundant fish, insects, reptiles, birds and plants, one of the richest Eocene fossil insect faunas.

title: Champsosaurs and kin die out

facts.text: Champsosaurus and its crocodile-like neochoristodere relatives, survivors of the K–Pg extinction, died out in the early Eocene.
Their loss coincides with the mammal turnover linked to PETM warmth.
Only the small lizard-like Lazarussuchus carried the choristodere line on, in Europe, until the Miocene.

facts.text: Gastornis, a large flightless bird, appears in the fossil record about 56 million years ago.
It went extinct about 40 million years ago.
Archicebus achilles, from about 55 million years ago, is the earliest known ancestor of primates.
In North America, tarsier-like omomyids and lemur-like strepsirrhines replaced the archaic plesiadapiforms at the start of the Eocene.
Primates were exchanged between North America and Asia around 55.8 million years ago.
Primates split into strepsirrhines (lemurs, lorises) and haplorhines (tarsiers, anthropoids) and diversified by about 50 million years ago.

image.caption: Andrea Jagher, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

title: Modern bird groups diversify (songbirds, parrots, loons)

facts.text: Many modern bird orders first appeared in the Eocene: the first songbirds, parrots, loons, swifts and woodpeckers.
The oldest known stem loon, Nasidytes, comes from England's London Clay, about 55 million years old.
The first perching birds (passerines) appear around 52.5 million years ago.
The woodpecker order dates from the early Eocene and the kingfisher order from the middle Eocene.

title: India collides with Asia; Himalayas begin to rise

facts.text: India's collision with the Eurasian plate is most often dated to about 55–50 million years ago, though the exact timing is debated.
India's northwestern corner touched Eurasia first, about 55 Ma; contact along the Yarlung–Zangbo suture began around 50 Ma.
India's plate slowed from about 18–19.5 cm a year to about 4.5 cm a year around 55 Ma, circumstantial evidence of the collision.
The collision closed the Tethys Ocean there and began thrusting up the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau.
Rival models have a microcontinent colliding first, with India itself arriving only around 40 Ma or even at the end of the Oligocene.

contested_note: The timing and nature of the India–Asia collision are debated, with models ranging from about 58 Ma to the end of the Oligocene.

title: Main phase of Pyrenean mountain building

facts.text: Iberia and Europe, converging since about 100 million years ago, collided in the Eocene and Oligocene.
From about 55 million years ago the Pyrenees underwent very strong crustal compression, which set up the range's present structure.
This main phase lasted until about 47 million years ago, shortening the crust by about 4 mm a year and stacking thrust sheets.

title: North Atlantic opens between Greenland and Europe
article: Opening of the North Atlantic Ocean

facts.text: Seafloor spreading crept north from the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay and, by about 54 million years ago, split Greenland from Eurasia.
The opening of the North Atlantic finally broke the old northern continent Laurasia in two.
By 56 million years ago Greenland was already its own plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift.
The North Atlantic Igneous Province's break-up volcanism ran from about 56 to 54 million years ago, forming the Iceland Plateau and Greenland's Skaergaard intrusion.
Extension between North America and Eurasia also opened the Eurasian Basin across the Arctic.

facts.text: Shallow seas over southeast England laid down the London Clay, rich in fossil seeds and fruits of some 350 plant species.
Its flora includes tropical plants now found in Asia, reflecting the much warmer early Eocene climate.

conflicts.note: Lagerstätte lists

facts.text: The EECO was a long spell of extreme greenhouse warmth, the warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic Era.
It was set off by a series of intense early Eocene hyperthermals, including ETM-2 and ETM-3.
Global mean surface temperature is estimated at about 23–30 °C; the 56–47 Ma hothouse ran about 14 °C warmer than today.
Antarctic summers reached about 25 °C, alligators and amphibians lived north of the Arctic Circle, and palms grew in Alaska.
Climate models struggle to reproduce its warm poles and mild polar winters, the so-called equable climate problem.

conflicts.note: PETM page (2020 study): EECO 53.3–49.1 Mya

facts.text: ETM-2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after the PETM.
It left a smaller drop in carbon-13 than the PETM and was less severe.
It came exactly 4.5 long orbital-eccentricity cycles after the PETM, and orbital forcing may have triggered it.
Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they ushered in the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

facts.text: Mountain building in the Rockies created basins in which Lakes Gosiute, Uinta and Fossil Lake laid down the oil shales of the Green River Formation.
Oxygen-poor lake-bottom muds slowed decay and kept scavengers away, preserving fish, leaves and even soft parts of insects.
It is perhaps the best record of Cenozoic freshwater communities, with fish, crocodilians, birds and mammals.
Frost-free climate let crocodiles live there among sycamore forests, as the moist early Eocene turned slightly drier.

conflicts.note: List of lagerstätten / Lagerstätte pages: single 50 Ma date

facts.text: The pakicetids, a family of hoofed land mammals, are the earliest whales; they lived about 53 million years ago.
Their closest known relative was Indohyus, of the family Raoellidae.
Pakicetids could already hear under water through bone conduction rather than eardrums.
Whales became very diverse during the Eocene, when they made the full transition from land to sea.

conflicts.note: Timeline of life: first whale (Himalayacetus) and first whale ancestors c. 55 Ma

facts.text: ETM-3, informally the K or X event, was another early Eocene hyperthermal marked by a pulse of isotopically light carbon.
Its carbon-isotope excursion marks the onset of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

conflicts.note: Paleogene page (cites 2010)
Hyperthermal event page (cites 2009)

facts.text: The first equids lived in North America by the earliest Eocene, with early equoids of unclear affinity in Europe.
Eohippus appeared about 52 million years ago, and one of its species branched out into various new types of horse.
Thousands of complete skeletons of these early horses come from Eocene layers, mainly in Wyoming's Wind River basin.
About 50 million years ago Eohippus graded into Orohippus, which gave rise to Epihippus, with better grinding teeth, about 47 million years ago.
Their European cousins, the palaeotheres, arose later in the early Eocene.

conflicts.note: Equoidea page: definite equoids by the earliest Eocene (unit-dated, 56–48.07 Ma)

facts.text: The earliest known bats, such as Onychonycteris, appear about 52 million years ago.
They arrived only about 16 million years after the non-avian dinosaurs died out.
With bats, mammals had colonized the air by the Eocene.
Bat lineages also crossed from Africa to South America during the Eocene, possibly by way of Antarctica.

conflicts.note: Mammal page (cites 2008): earliest known bat about 50 Ma

facts.text: Amber from Gujarat, India, preserves an important early Eocene assemblage of arthropods, mainly insects.

verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

facts.text: Lakes in the uplands of British Columbia and Washington preserved detailed plants, insects and fish through the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.
Fossil palm beetles at McAbee, dated to about 52.9 million years, show palms grew in these uplands.
The 48.7-million-year-old Princeton Chert preserves plants in anatomical detail, with the oldest known ectomycorrhizal fungi.
The ancestors of cats and of dogs diverged about 50 million years ago, among the first true carnivorans.
Arctoids, the bear, weasel and raccoon branch, are known on all continents from 46 million years ago.
Early carnivorans stayed small while oxyaenids and mesonychians held the top-predator roles in the Eocene.
Crown-group carnivorans first appeared around 42 million years ago.
Deformation in the Sevier fold-and-thrust belt of western North America, under way since about 160 million years ago, ended around 50 Ma.
In southwestern Utah some Sevier thrusts may have stayed active until later in the Eocene.

conflicts.note: Sevier page: belt active through the Eocene

facts.text: Near Verona, Italy, low-oxygen mud preserved fish so well that their organs are often intact and skin colour can sometimes be read.
Its Pesciara ('fishbowl') is famous for extraordinarily well preserved Eocene fish.

title: Ambulocetus: whales take to the water

facts.text: Ambulocetus, a probably amphibious, crocodile-like early whale, lived about 49 million years ago.
Ambulocetids lived in the bays and estuaries of the Tethys Ocean in what is now northern Pakistan.
By about 49 million years ago, whales had returned to the water.
Around 49 million years ago the warming climate turned to cooling, a slow trend that lasted until about 34 million years ago.
Changing geography and ocean circulation, as Australia and South America drew away from Antarctica, drove the drop.
Cold-water diatoms suggest winter sea ice formed in the Arctic, and Antarctica shows glaciation by about 37 million years ago.
Falling carbon dioxide, drawn down by organic productivity and weathering of new mountains, kept the cooling going; models suggest CO2 mattered more than ocean isolation.
The cooling that began in the middle Eocene ultimately led to the ice ages of the Quaternary.

conflicts.note: Cenozoic page: long-term cooling from about 50 Ma
Eocene page: shift to cooler climate at the end of the EECO

facts.text: With the Arctic Ocean almost cut off from the wider oceans, warm waters and high carbon dioxide let the floating fern Azolla grow rapidly across it.
With modest warmth and 20 hours of polar summer daylight, the fern can double its biomass in two to three days.
Dead ferns sank to the stagnant seafloor and were buried in sediment over about 800,000 years, building large Azolla deposits that locked away carbon.
Carbon dioxide fell catastrophically, from about 3,500 ppm in the early Eocene to 650 ppm during the event.
The drawdown is believed to have ended the early Eocene warmth about 48.5 Ma; temperatures fell rapidly 49-47 Ma, and glacial dropstones then became common in Arctic sediments.

conflicts.note: PETM page: Azolla deposits in the middle Eocene (unit-dated, 48.07–37.71 Ma)

title: Lutetian limestone (Paris stone) forms

facts.text: In the middle Lutetian a sea over the Paris Basin laid down marine limestone, later topped by freshwater limestone and marl once the sea withdrew.
The Lutetian age, 48.07–41.03 million years ago, is named after this limestone, from Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris.
Used since Roman times, this 'Paris stone' built many of the city's grandest buildings, including parts of the Louvre and the Arc de Triomphe.

title: European Cenozoic Rift System opens

facts.text: The ongoing Alpine collision opened a north–south rift system across western Europe from the Eocene onward.
The Limagne Graben formed in the middle Eocene, holding a lake, and rifting also began in the Bresse Graben.

title: First savannas as grasses spread

facts.text: Grasses began to spread as the climate cooled and dried after the EECO; subhumid savannas are known in South America from the middle Eocene.
Grasses moved out from riverbanks into open tracts during the Eocene.

facts.text: The Kula plate, subducting under Alaska and the Yukon since the early Eocene, was entirely consumed around 48 million years ago.
Only a slab in the mantle under the Bering Sea remains.

conflicts.note: Paleogene page (cites 2017): Kula–Pacific spreading ceased c. 40 Ma and the Kula plate joined the Pacific plate

facts.text: A coastal moorland of lakes and tidal bays in central Germany preserved over 50,000 fossil vertebrates, plus insects and plants.
Its soft tissues were among the very first found from the Eocene, and its mammals define a European land-mammal stage.

conflicts.note: List of lagerstätten (cites 2024)

title: Polar forests in the Canadian Arctic

facts.text: High-Arctic river deposits in Nunavut preserve old-growth conifer forests where they grew, with leaf litter preserved down to the molecular level.
Swamp cypress and dawn redwood grew on Ellesmere Island, and subtropical plants in Greenland and Alaska.
Pollen from Prydz Bay shows taiga forest grew in Antarctica too.
A lake at Messel, in Hesse, Germany, preserved over 1,400 taxa of plants and animals about 47 million years ago, the best record of its time.
Near the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, the site had a mean annual temperature of 22 °C, with maar lakes ringed by lush subtropical forest; it lay 10° farther south.
Animals sank into deep, oxygen-poor water without scavengers, so whole skeletons survive, some even with fur, feathers and 'skin shadows'.
Bursts of toxic volcanic gas from the lake, like Lake Nyos in 1986, may have killed the animals; other researchers blame toxic cyanobacterial blooms.
Its fossils, from pygmy horses and early primates to bats, keep yielding major discoveries about the early evolution of mammals and birds.

conflicts.note: K–Ar date quoted on the Geiseltal page

title: Pacific plate turns: the Hawaiian–Emperor bend

facts.text: A kink in the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain marks the Pacific plate's sudden swing from northward to northwestward motion about 47 million years ago.
The change followed the onset of subduction along the plate's western edge.
A wider reorganisation of Pacific plate motions started the Izu-Bonin-Mariana and Tonga-Kermadec subduction zones.
The end of a northward pull around 47 Ma, the hotspot's southward drift from about 50 Ma and new western subduction zones together may explain the bend.

conflicts.note: Sharp and Clague: bend starting about 50 Ma

title: Baltic amber forest

facts.text: The largest amber deposit on Earth, and the biggest single store of fossil insects, preserves invertebrates, plants and small vertebrates of subtropical eastern Europe.
Its exact age is controversial; estimates include 47–40 and 43–35 million years.
Two other major European ambers, from Bitterfeld in Germany and Rovno in Ukraine, date to 38–34 million years ago and share much of its fauna.

contested_note: The age of Baltic amber within the Eocene is controversial.

facts.text: Oil shale in Montana preserves exquisitely detailed insects, including a blood-filled mosquito with traces of hemoglobin.

title: Silverpit crater (possible impact)

facts.text: A buried crater-like structure lies under the North Sea, about 130 km off the Humber estuary.
A 2025 study argues it is an impact crater about 3.2 km wide, ringed by an 18 km disturbed zone, formed 46–43 million years ago.
Others attribute it to salt movement, an explanation favoured in a 2009 debate.

contested_note: Its impact origin is disputed; a salt-withdrawal origin was long judged more plausible.

title: Andes: Incaic phase and rise of the Altiplano

facts.text: The Altiplano began to form in the Eocene as subduction beneath South America compressed the plate margin.
The high Central Andes and the Bolivian orocline formed from about 45 million years ago; major uplift in southern Peru began then too.
In northern Peru the Incaic phase of Andean mountain building struck in the middle and late Eocene.
Uplift of Peru's Western Cordillera had begun about 50 million years ago, then paused until the Oligocene.
The region around the Altiplano and Puna plateaus has been shortened horizontally ever since.

title: Tasmanian Passage: Australia pulls away from Antarctica

facts.text: When Australia split from Antarctica around 45 million years ago, warm equatorial currents were diverted and a cold-water channel opened between them.
The South Tasman Rise had already sunk beneath the sea, forming the Tasmanian Passage.
As oceanic crust began separating the continents about 35.5 million years ago, global ocean temperatures dropped significantly.
The general consensus is that the two continents had fully separated by 60 million years ago; 45 Ma is a minority estimate.

contested_note: Sources disagree on when Australia fully separated from Antarctica, from 60 Ma (consensus) to 45 Ma or later.

facts.text: Karst fissure deposits in southern France hold mammals, birds, turtles, crocodiles, plants and insects.
Some amphibians and lizards are preserved as articulated 'natural mummies' with soft tissue.
The Indo-Australian plate formed when the Indian and Australian plates fused, approximately 43 million years ago.
A meteorite impact near Lahoysk, Belarus, about 42.3 million years ago left a 15 km crater, now buried.
Around 42 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field flipped 17 times in 3 million years.
Earlier, in a 4-million-year window centred on 54 Ma, there were 10 reversals.
Basilosaurus, a large predatory archaeocete whale, lived from about 41.3 to 33.9 million years ago.
At 17–20 m and up to 15 tonnes, it was one of the largest animals of the Paleogene.
A top predator of shallow seas, it ate sharks, large fish and other marine mammals, especially the smaller whale Dorudon.
By the end of the Eocene, whales such as Basilosaurus had become fully aquatic.
Its extinction coincides with the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, which ended almost all other archaeocetes.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: Basilosaurus evolves c. 40 Ma

title: Drake Passage begins to open

facts.text: In the early Eocene the Drake Passage was only a small opening with limited circulation.
Sediments suggest it began opening about 41 million years ago, while tectonic evidence points to about 32 million years ago.
The Scotia plate began forming about 40 million years ago, breaking a continuous landmass from Patagonia to the Antarctic Peninsula.
Cooling during the passage's first opening, about 38.5 million years ago, was not global: the North Atlantic did not cool.
The Drake and Tasmanian passages ended the Antarctic land bridge in the late Eocene or early Oligocene.

contested_note: The timing of the Drake Passage opening is uncertain, with estimates from 49 to 17 million years ago.

facts.text: From about 40.5 to 40.0 million years ago, a spell of very warm climate briefly reversed the long Middle–Late Eocene cooling.
The warming was globally synchronous; mean surface temperature reached about 23 °C and Tethys sea surfaces 32–36 °C.
Carbon dioxide, not methane, drove it; one estimate puts CO2 at 4,000 ppm, though other studies find a smaller rise.
A coinciding minimum in two orbital eccentricity cycles, around 40.2 million years ago, likely helped sustain the warmth.
Planktonic foraminifera turned over: acarinids dwindled and morozovellids went extinct.

verification.title: Coupled greenhouse warming and deep‐sea acidification in the middle Eocene

facts.text: About 50 million years ago Eurasia was split into three landmasses: Western Europe, Balkanatolia and Asia.
Balkanatolia joined Asia about 40 million years ago; Europe connected only about 34 million years ago.
Invading Asian mammals may have driven Balkanatolia's island-like endemic fauna extinct.

title: Eridanos, the Baltic river, begins to form

facts.text: The Eridanos, an ancient river that flowed through what is now the Baltic Sea, began to form about 40 million years ago.

title: Mesohippus: horses adapt to open country

facts.text: About 40 million years ago Mesohippus appeared suddenly, under strong new selective pressures.
Late Eocene horses grew tougher teeth and became larger and leggier, able to outrun predators in open country.
Miohippus followed around 36 million years ago.

title: Rodents and monkeys raft from Africa to South America

facts.text: About 40 million years ago caviomorph rodents reached South America, most likely from Africa.
Primates followed from Africa by 36 million years ago, crossing in the same way.
The ocean gap was narrower then; animals floated over on driftwood or mangrove rafts, perhaps island-hopping.
The rodents gave rise to capybaras, chinchillas and New World porcupines, displacing some small marsupials.
Today the descendants of these rafters make up more than twice as many South American species as those of older native mammals.

conflicts.note: Agua de la Piedra page: first rodents arrived in the Late Eocene (unit-dated)
Caviomorphs reached Patagonia in the latest Eocene or early Oligocene

verification.title: Arrival and Diversification of Caviomorph Rodents and Platyrrhine Primates in South America

facts.text: Volcanism and rifting began around Turkana in northern Kenya 40–35 million years ago, then spread north and south along the Gregory Rift.
From about 40 to 25 million years ago a dramatic burst of volcanic eruptions swept the western United States.
Its andesite-to-rhyolite eruptions produced about 500,000 km³ of explosive and 5 million km³ of effusive volcanic rock.
It followed the end of Laramide compression, as the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion changed.
Volcanoes of Colorado's San Juan field became active 40–35 million years ago; New Mexico's Mogollon-Datil field began erupting about 36.2 million years ago.
In Mexico's Sierra Madre Occidental, the flare-up's Oligocene ash flows stacked ignimbrite sheets covering the largest area of any known series, with ten calderas.

title: Last multituberculates

facts.text: Multituberculates, rodent-like mammals that had declined since the mid-Paleocene, finally went extinct in the late Eocene.
The last species, Ectypodus childei, died out in North America near the end of the Eocene, possibly outcompeted by rodents.
Around 35 million years ago, extinctions also struck gastropods, reptiles and amphibians.
This ancient lineage dated back to the Jurassic; only the gondwanatheres outlived it.
They had dominated most mammal assemblages for at least 88 million years; one account has them lasting into the early Oligocene.

facts.text: An impact about 37.2 million years ago made an 8.4 km crater, now filled by Lake Wanapitei.
Volcanism in the Cascade arc of the Pacific Northwest began about 37 million years ago.
The West Cascades period, 37 to 17 million years ago, was a time of exceptionally active volcanoes.

title: First ice sheets grow on Antarctica

facts.text: By the late Eocene, about 37 million years ago, temperatures had fallen enough for ice sheets to start forming in Antarctica.
Oxygen isotopes show ice building up from about 36 million years ago, and permanent ice from about 35 million years ago.
Around 35 million years ago, glaciers merged into the East Antarctic Ice Sheet, burying the Gamburtsev Mountains.
A brief glaciation, the Late Eocene Event, followed about 34.4 million years ago.

conflicts.note: Geological history of Earth: present pattern of ice ages began about 40 Ma
Miocene page (cites 2016): ice began to build up

title: White River fauna: modern rodents take over

facts.text: In North America's Chadronian age, from 37 million years ago, the White River fauna was in full swing.
Modern rodent families such as beavers, squirrels and gophers replaced older tropical ones, alongside early relatives of bears, peccaries and rabbits.
Rabbit relatives, first found in East Asia, reached North America in the late Eocene.
An impact in Labrador, Canada, about 36.6 million years ago left a crater originally about 28 km across.
A large bolide blasted a 100 km crater in northern Siberia in the late Eocene.
It is tied as the fourth-largest verified impact structure on Earth.
It may be linked to the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, and may have struck at the same time as the Chesapeake Bay and Toms Canyon impacts.

conflicts.note: Popigai lead text

facts.text: A bolide about 3 km wide struck the eastern shore of North America, then lined with rainforest and shallow limy seas.
It left a crater about 85 km wide, now buried beneath the mouth of Chesapeake Bay.
It is one of the best-preserved marine-target craters, and sediment slumping over its rubble helped shape the bay.
The nearby Toms Canyon crater, and possibly Siberia's Popigai, may have formed in the same event.

conflicts.note: Eocene page (cites 2008, 2004)

title: Laramide orogeny ends

facts.text: The Laramide orogeny, which raised mountains across western North America from the Late Cretaceous, ended sometime between 55 and 35 million years ago.
Compression gave way to crustal extension that ultimately formed the Basin and Range Province.
As convergence slowed the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion turned oblique, and volcanism flared across the Basin and Range.
In New Mexico, Laramide deformation lasted until about 40 million years ago.
The orogeny's exact start and end dates are in dispute.

contested_note: The Laramide orogeny's end is dated anywhere from 56 to 35 million years ago, and its exact timing is in dispute.

facts.text: About 35 million years ago Adria's Anatolide–Tauride platform entered the subduction trench, beginning the Dinarides, Hellenides and Taurides.
Between about 40 and 30 million years ago, subduction began along the western Mediterranean arc of the Tell, Rif, Betic and Apennine chains.
The Central and Western Alps formed in a second orogenic phase starting at the end of the Eocene, 35 million years ago.

title: Pacific Ring of Fire takes modern shape

facts.text: By about 35 million years ago the Kula and Farallon plates had been subducted, and the Pacific plate was ringed by subduction much like today's Ring of Fire.
The New Zealand subduction zone, the last of its present segments, formed about 35 million years ago.

title: Arabia collides with Eurasia; Zagros begin to rise

facts.text: Continental collision between Arabia and Eurasia began about 35 million years ago and continued into the Oligocene, to about 26 million years ago.
It closed the Tethys Ocean there and created the Zagros Mountains.
Earlier, a subducted slab of Neotethys ocean floor had broken off near the Arabian margin during the Eocene.

title: EOT-1: first step of Antarctic glaciation

facts.text: Long cooling crossed a threshold around 34 million years ago, and a large ice sheet formed in East Antarctica as carbon dioxide fell.
Antarctica glaciated in two steps; the first and smaller, EOT-1, came about 34.1–33.9 million years ago, at the boundary itself.
By the boundary an ice sheet in western Antarctica reached the ocean, and glaciers had appeared in Greenland.
Glaciers sliding off the Gamburtsev Mountains are thought to have seeded the East Antarctic Ice Sheet.
At the Eocene–Oligocene transition, about 34 million years ago, deep overturning circulation shifted from the Pacific to the Atlantic as the Arctic–Atlantic gateway closed.

facts.text: In Colorado, diatom blooms in a lake dammed by volcanic mudflows finely preserved late Eocene plants and insects.
The site is also known for petrified stumps of giant sequoia relatives.
The ancestors of toothed and baleen whales split around 34 million years ago, as the southern oceans' climate changed with the opening of the Drake Passage.
The earliest known mysticete, Mystacodon, 37 to 33 million years old, still had teeth and fed by suction.
Later forms carried both baleen and teeth, then lost their teeth and became full filter feeders, as all living baleen whales are.
Toothed whales are defined by features for echolocation, such as a fatty melon; Oligocene Squalodon skulls give the first hypothesized evidence of it.

facts.text: The Eocene ends with a major extinction and faunal turnover, called the Grande Coupure in Europe, spanning about 33.9 to 33.4 million years ago.
It accompanied Earth's shift from greenhouse to icehouse: sharp cooling, a big sea-level drop and rapid growth of the Antarctic ice sheet as CO2 fell to about 750–800 ppm.
The extinction of hantkeninid planktonic foraminifera marks the boundary; Basilosaurus and nearly all other archaic whales died out.
Cooling turned over snails, amphibians and reptiles in central North America; some sites show extinctions drawn out over millions of years, starting in the early Priabonian.
Its causes are debated and not fully understood; the large Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts may also be involved.
